What does a car really cost? Map the loan, running costs and resale value

Use four graphics to connect the monthly commitment with the full cost of ownership and the risk of owing more than the car is worth.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore the full cost of owning a car

Interactive planning lab

Initial monthly cash outflow$1,103.18
Net cost over selected years$59,685.56
Sale value less remaining loan$15,529.69

Hypothetical financed purchase, not a lease or lender quote. Acquisition taxes and fees are entered separately; down payment applies to the total. Fixed loan rate uses nominal annual rate divided by 12, with month-end payments and no balloon or extra financing charges. Vehicle value declines at a constant annual percentage; running costs rise once a year. Exit assumes sale at modeled value and full repayment of remaining principal, with no sale fees, prepayment costs or taxes at sale. No investment opportunity cost is included.

The central idea

The monthly loan payment is one cash-flow component. A full plan also includes acquisition costs, running costs, the ownership period and debt remaining when you sell.

01

Separate the vehicle’s value from the amount financed

The example starts with a vehicle purchase value and adds acquisition taxes and fees as a separate input. The down payment applies to that combined purchase cost. The loan finances the remainder, while the vehicle’s starting modeled resale value excludes those acquisition costs.

In the default case, a CAD 35,000 vehicle plus CAD 4,000 of entered costs requires CAD 39,000. A 20% down payment is CAD 7,800, leaving CAD 31,200 financed. This distinction prevents a tax or fee payment from automatically appearing as additional vehicle value.

All amounts are hypothetical, including the acquisition-cost allowance. They are not a dealer quote or a calculation of provincial taxes. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s financing overview describes different ways of financing a car; this tool models a fully amortizing purchase loan.

02

Build the recurring cash requirement

The default loan uses a 6% nominal annual rate divided by twelve, with equal month-end payments over five years. The scheduled monthly payment is CAD 603.18. Adding CAD 500 of initial running costs gives a first-month recurring requirement of CAD 1,103.18, before the separate down payment.

Running costs can include insurance, fuel or charging, parking, maintenance and other regular vehicle expenses. Use a budget based on the vehicle and expected usage. A fixed monthly allowance simplifies the chart; actual repair bills can be uneven and may need their own periodic-bill reserve.

The model increases running costs once per year at the selected rate. The loan payment remains fixed until the loan is repaid, then stops. A payment comparison that omits those timing changes can understate the ongoing commitment or assume loan payments continue after the debt has reached zero.

03

Compare the asset path with the debt path

The first chart follows vehicle value and remaining loan principal over the selected ownership period. Vehicle value declines at a constant assumed percentage each year. The debt follows the amortization schedule, which depends on the balance, rate and loan term.

If debt exceeds modeled vehicle value, the household has negative equity at that date. Selling for that value would leave part of the loan to be funded from elsewhere. The FCAC’s discussion of car-financing risks explains negative equity and why long repayment terms deserve attention.

Try a longer loan term and a faster value decline. A smaller monthly payment can coexist with more debt at the intended sale date. The depreciation assumption here is independently selected and smooth. It is not an appraisal, a source-reported depreciation schedule or a forecast of used-car prices.

04

Reconcile what leaves the household over the whole period

The waterfall adds the down payment, loan payments made during ownership and running costs. It then adds the loan balance that must be settled at sale and subtracts the vehicle’s modeled sale proceeds. The endpoint is the net cash cost of owning and exiting under these assumptions.

For the default five-year case, the net cost is CAD 59,685.56. The same result can be checked as vehicle value lost, plus acquisition costs, plus loan interest, plus running costs. The remaining loan is zero at that endpoint because the ownership period matches the repayment term.

These are two ways of describing the same cost. Adding depreciation again to the waterfall would count the loss of vehicle value twice. If the car is sold before the loan ends, include the remaining principal in the settlement; subtracting the full vehicle value while ignoring that debt would overstate the cash recovered.

05

Review the exit date as well as the payment

The matrix varies the loan rate and term while retaining the selected ownership horizon. Each cell settles any remaining debt at that date. The displayed amounts are total ownership costs, so they should not be read as monthly payments or as interest bills alone.

At a positive rate, extending repayment can lower the scheduled payment while increasing the interest incurred before a given exit. At zero interest, different terms change the timing of principal payments, but settling the remaining balance at sale keeps the underlying principal cost consistent.

The tool excludes investment opportunity cost, selling expenses, prepayment costs, balloon payments, insurance claims and differences between quoted and realized resale value. Review the actual financing contract, purchase costs and a realistic operating budget. Connect the commitment with the household’s other goals and its ability to handle an earlier-than-planned sale.
